subject: Evaluating access conduits for on-prem private deployment — telemetry & ops impact
messages:
From: Oliver Brooks <oliver.brooks@everwellrx.com>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
Cc: Rajiv Singh <rajiv.singh@everwellrx.com>
Date: Thu, 12 Nov 2026 09:18:00 -0800
Subject: Access conduit options for our on‑prem LLM private deployment

Stephanie —

Thanks again for the demo yesterday. As we prep our private deployment (on‑prem inference clusters behind our firewall), our security team has pushed back on the connectivity options. They want a clear recommendation: VPC peering (cross‑account peering to our cloud anchor), PrivateLink/Interface Endpoint, or an IPsec site‑to‑site VPN. Primary concerns are:
- Zero‑trust posture (least privileged egress)
- Stable egress IPs for allow‑listing
- Observability & telemetry into request/latency/error metrics
- Maintenance/operational overhead for our infra team
- Cost predictability

Could you outline operational impacts for each path and any telemetry blind spots we should expect? We have a narrow window for go‑live at end of Q4. Attached a short network diagram. 

—Oliver
Director of Cloud Architecture
EverwellRx
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
To: Oliver Brooks <oliver.brooks@everwellrx.com>
Cc: Rajiv Singh <rajiv.singh@everwellrx.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>, Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 12 Nov 2026 10:07:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Access conduit options for our on‑prem LLM private deployment

Oliver —

Appreciate the clear ask. I attached a short decision matrix (20261112-access-matrix.xlsx) and a quick diagram that maps each path to operational/telemetry impact (privatelink‑vs‑peering‑diagram.png).

High level preview:
- VPC peering: low latency, preserves source IPs inside cloud VPCs; however, cross‑account peering requires careful routing and does not provide an endpoint with fixed egress IPs on the customer side — you'd need NAT/egress addresses at your edge. Telemetry: full visibility in our control plane + VPC flow logs, but requires coordinating with your netops for end‑to‑end tracing.

- PrivateLink: gives you per‑endpoint interface ENIs and stable endpoint IPs in your VPC; good for allow‑listing and simpler ownership boundaries. Telemetry: we get connection metrics at the interface level but prefix/KV cache visibility is reduced unless we extend tracing headers and propagate request ids — ops work but manageable.

- Site‑to‑Site VPN (IPsec): easiest to stand up without cross‑account cloud changes; predictable public egress IPs from your firewall. Downside: higher latency jitter, potential MTU and fragmentation issues, and more operational toil (tunnel upkeep, rekeying). Telemetry: blind spots for per‑stream request tracing unless you inject tracing across the tunnel; packet drops can be hard to correlate to application errors.

Can Neha and Jordan add a quick note on auth/token flow constraints and long‑running streaming sessions? If you can share which of these constraints (eg: strict egress IPs vs lowest latency) are absolute, we can prioritize. I'd propose a 30‑minute call tomorrow to align. 

—Stephanie
Head of Solutions, Redwood Inference
From: Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
Cc: Oliver Brooks <oliver.brooks@everwellrx.com>, Rajiv Singh <rajiv.singh@everwellrx.com>, Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>
Date: Thu, 12 Nov 2026 14:22:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Access conduit options for our on‑prem LLM private deployment

On Thu, Nov 12, 2026 at 10:07 AM Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai> wrote:
> Can Neha and Jordan add a quick note on auth/token flow constraints and long‑running streaming sessions?

Quick technical notes from my side:

1) Auth & tokens — our hosted control plane issues short‑lived server tokens for model attachments. For PrivateLink and peering, we can validate requests using mTLS + short bearer tokens; for VPN there is no additional handshake so you must ensure your perimeter performs token validation before NAT. If your edge terminates TLS and does bearer token inspection, we lose request‑level cryptographic identity unless we proxy.

2) Streaming sessions — PrivateLink and peering preserve TCP characteristics better than VPN. VPNs can introduce rekey events/packet loss that break long‑lived HTTP/2 or streaming websocket sessions; we often see session resets that require retry logic. For low‑latency interactive apps (sub‑100ms), peering is preferable.

3) Telemetry/Tracing — to get full per‑request traces across customer network + Redwood runtime we rely on propagated trace headers (x-request-id / traceparent). With PrivateLink you can get consistent mapping because the interface endpoint sits in your VPC; with peering you'll need to ensure route tables + NAT do not rewrite source headers. With VPN you must instrument your edge device to preserve or propagate headers.

4) Egress IPs — If allow‑listing is non‑negotiable, PrivateLink is the simplest for predictable host addresses (ENI IPs), otherwise you can front with a fixed egress NAT gateway.

I'll join the call if we schedule one. 

—Neha
Senior Product Engineer, Redwood
From: Rajiv Singh <rajiv.singh@everwellrx.com>
To: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
Cc: Oliver Brooks <oliver.brooks@everwellrx.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 13 Nov 2026 08:43:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Access conduit options for our on‑prem LLM private deployment

Thanks — helpful writeup. A couple clarifying points from our security team:

- Allow‑listing external hosts: Our legal/compliance team requires that third‑party outbound hosts be fixed and documented. We prefer conservative posture — predictable IPs are mandatory.
- SLA and failover: We need to understand Redwood's failure modes and RTO if a PrivateLink endpoint fails vs if a peering path gets blackholed.
- Cost: we will be charged egress and interface fees either way; please include any support hours we should budget for operations handoffs.

If PrivateLink gives us fixed ENI IPs and simpler allow‑listing, what are the tradeoffs for cross‑region deployments? We're planning an active‑active footprint (east/west). 

—Rajiv
Network Architect, EverwellRx
From: Stephanie Nguyen <stephanie_nguyen@redwood.ai>
To: Rajiv Singh <rajiv.singh@everwellrx.com>
Cc: Oliver Brooks <oliver.brooks@everwellrx.com>, Neha Kapoor <neha_kapoor@redwood.ai>, Jordan Blake <jordan_blake@redwood.ai>
Date: Fri, 13 Nov 2026 16:02:00 -0800
Subject: Re: Access conduit options for our on‑prem LLM private deployment

Rajiv / Oliver —

Thanks — concrete answers below to help your compliance review and budgeting:

1) Fixed IPs / allow‑listing
- PrivateLink: provides ENIs per AZ/VPC with stable private IPs inside your VPC. For public allow‑listing we can front the endpoint behind a small egress NAT in your VPC that uses an elastic IP per region — that gives you predictable public egress addresses. This is the recommended approach for strict allow‑listing with minimal app changes.
- Peering: does not provide a public stable egress automatically. You'd need a managed NAT or dedicated egress fleet (maintained by you) to present stable public IPs.
- VPN: your firewall provides stable egress IPs but you inherit the VPN maintenance burden.

2) Failure modes & RTO
- PrivateLink: if an interface ENI in an AZ becomes unhealthy, traffic will failover to other AZs if you provision multi‑AZ endpoints; failover is usually quick but depends on DNS/IP health checks and your route configuration. Redwood can provide runbook and SLA addendum for endpoint monitoring and support hours.
- Peering: route misconfigurations can cause more silent failures; detection relies on BGP/static route health checks — RTO can be longer unless you instrument flows and synthetic traffic.
- VPN: tunnel outages are visible at the tunnel level but can flake; RTO depends on your edge redundancy.

3) Cross‑region / active‑active
- PrivateLink: endpoints are regional; for active‑active you'll provision endpoints per region and use DNS/route weights to steer traffic. Slightly more operational setup but gives clean isolation by region.
- Peering: cross‑region peering (e.g., inter‑VPC across accounts/regions) is supported but increases routing complexity.

4) Estimated support/ops budget
- We recommend initial integration support (2–3 days) for PrivateLink (setting up endpoint configs, tracing headers, test harness), plus a runbook handoff. VPN or peering may require more netops hours on your side.

Recommendation summary: For EverwellRx's compliance needs (predictable egress + easier allow‑listing) PrivateLink + regional egress NAT is the lowest‑risk path. If you need the absolute lowest latency for interactive streams and can coordinate routing, peering is an option but requires more joint ops work to guarantee stable public egress and trace continuity.

Next steps: if you agree, we'll draft an operations playbook and schedule a 45‑minute technical walkthrough with your netops and our SRE team next week. 

Thanks —

Stephanie Nguyen
Head of Solutions, Redwood Inference

Attachments: 20261112-access-matrix.xlsx (decision matrix), privatelink-vs-peering-diagram.png
